name: Touriga Nacional

lines.s10: Touriga Nacional is the backbone of Port and the Douro's dry reds: blackberry and violet with a lift of bergamot.
lines.s20: Touriga Nacional is the red grape at the heart of Port and of Portugal's dry reds, from the Douro and the Dão. It is deep purple and full, with blackberry and violet, a lift of bergamot and a firm, velvety tannin.
lines.s45: Touriga Nacional gives Port its backbone, and it leads many of Portugal's dry reds. It was born in the Dão, they say near the village of Tourigo, and made its name in the Douro. The glass is nearly black, with blackberry, violet and a lift of bergamot. It is full in body, with a firm, velvety tannin. Its small, thick skinned berries give that depth, and time in French oak rounds it out. The Dão makes it finer and more perfumed, the Douro fuller. It suits roast lamb, game or hard cheese. Bordeaux now trials it as its summers grow hotter.
lines.sale: Touriga Nacional is Port's own grape made dry: all the blackberry and violet, none of the sweetness, with a bergamot lift that keeps it bright. Decanted now, it will be ready for the lamb or the game.

glass.lead: Blackberry, blueberry and violet with a lift of bergamot, nearly opaque and full bodied, over a firm, velvety tannin.

ladder.where: The Dão's granite plateau and Bairrada
The Douro's schist, the Alentejo and Rutherglen

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, tannin high and velvety, alcohol medium plus, body full, and nearly opaque in colour.

home.home: Portugal. The Dão claims its birth near Tourigo, and on that granite plateau it is finer and more perfumed; in the Douro's schist it is fuller and leads both Port and the dry reds. Since the 1990s it has spread south to Lisboa, the Tejo and the Alentejo.
home.abroad: Rutherglen in Australia grows it for vintage fortified wine with Shiraz and Durif, South Africa's Little Karoo for fortified and dry reds, and Bordeaux has allowed it on trial since 2021.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as for any full red or Vintage Port.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass for the dry wines; a small tulip for Port.
service.decant: Consider it for a young dry red after tasting a sample; decant a Vintage Port off its crust.
service.age: The serious dry reds keep ten years and more; Vintage Port lasts for decades.

blackberry and a firm grip suit dark, rich meat

labels.means: The Port valley's dry wines, often blends led by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca.

guest.q: Is this the grape they make Port from?
guest.a: Yes, one of the main ones. This wine fermented all the way to dry, so you have the blackberry and violet of Port without its sweetness or the added grape spirit.

guest.q: Why does it smell faintly of orange peel?
guest.a: That lift is typical of Touriga Nacional: bergamot and orange peel over the blackberry and violet. It keeps a full, dark wine smelling bright.

guest.q: Which is better, the Douro or the Dão?
guest.a: Different, not better. The Douro's hot schist gives a fuller, darker wine; the Dão's cooler granite plateau gives more perfume, finer tannin and a little less weight.

compare.tell: Touriga Franca, its child, is lighter and juicier, with rose petal and pomegranate; Touriga Nacional is darker and firmer, with violet and bergamot.
Syrah brings cracked black pepper, black olive and smoked meat; Touriga Nacional has no such savoury side, and bergamot and orange peel lift its blackberry.
Malbec shares the violet and the dark colour but lacks the bergamot lift, and its tannin is softer and plusher than Touriga Nacional's firm grip.

cards.front: Touriga Nacional: which two Portuguese regions are home, and how do they differ?
cards.back: The Dão, where it is said to have been born and is finer and more perfumed, and the Douro, where it is fuller and leads Port and the dry reds.

cards.front: Touriga Nacional blind: which aromas give it away beside its blackberry?
cards.back: Violet with a lift of bergamot and orange peel, sometimes rockrose, over deep blackberry and black plum and a firm, velvety tannin.

cards.front: Why did Touriga Nacional nearly vanish, and what brought it back?
cards.back: Its small berries give very low yields, so growers chose other grapes after phylloxera. Research in the Douro in the 1970s and 1980s named it among five favoured Port grapes.

questions.q: A dry red poured blind is nearly opaque and full bodied, with blackberry, violet and a striking lift of bergamot, a firm, velvety tannin and fresh acidity. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Violet with a bergamot lift over deep blackberry marks Touriga Nacional. Malbec, the nearest miss, shares the violet and the colour but not the bergamot, and its tannin is softer.

questions.q: A guest who loves Vintage Port asks for a dry red led by the same main grape. Which bottle do you bring?
opts: A Douro red led by Touriga Nacional
A Bairrada red led by Baga
An Alentejo red led by Alicante Bouschet
A Setúbal red led by Castelão
questions.exp: Touriga Nacional is a main Port grape and leads many dry Douro reds. Baga, the nearest miss, is Bairrada's own grape and plays no part in Port.

questions.q: A guest notices Touriga Nacional among the grapes Bordeaux has allowed on trial since 2021 and asks why it was chosen. What do you tell him?
opts: It copes with heat and drought
It ripens early in cool, wet years
It gives a pale, light red
It is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.exp: Bordeaux admitted it on trial against a warming climate, and in the Douro it thrives where heat and drought are the hazards. Ripening early in cool years, the nearest wrong answer, is not its strength.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; nothing contradicts TASTE.world old, and the ladder's moderate and warm rungs follow TASTE.clim warm and the Codex's Dão record, which calls the plateau's reds fresher than the Douro's.

Port and the dry Douro reds, the small, thick skinned berries and low yields, the five favoured grapes chosen by research in the 1970s and 1980s, the Dão's claim to its birth near Tourigo, finer and more perfumed there, French oak, the spread south since the 1990s, Rutherglen with Shiraz and Durif, Bordeaux's trial grapes of 2021 against a warming climate, Stilton with Vintage Port and lamb and kid with Dão all stand on the Codex's own Douro, Dão, Lisboa, Tejo, Alentejo, Rutherglen and Bordeaux records and on GRAPES.

The near loss after phylloxera for its low yields stands on the Oxford Companion and on two trade pages seen through search; the Little Karoo on a Stellenbosch University thesis and on South African trade pages that name producers and so are not cited.

The Codex's Régionale trap calls Touriga Nacional Portugal's top red, a ranking the house rules keep out of new prose. GRAPES gives blueberry, which the lead keeps; the notes carry no blue fruit group for want of a second blue note in the sources.
This session reached search alone; no host could be fetched, so each address is cited as the search results gave it and a checker should open them.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. Port, the Dao's claim to its birth, the five favoured grapes, Rutherglen, the Little Karoo and Bordeaux's trial all stand; warm schist was a soil and not a note, a spoken line had the nose find a grip, two food reasons named no fruit, and the Port question offered Vinhao, which is Sousao and a Port grape.
changed: lines.s10: The line said the grape smells of violet and bergamot over a firm grip, and a grip is not smelled. It now brings blackberry and violet with bergamot on a firm grip, 25 words, one breath.

glass.notes: The mineral group held slate and warm schist. Warm schist is a soil warmed by the sun, not a note a taster can point to; the Codex's Douro record calls the dry reds schist scented, so schist stays, plain. The first round dropped the group, and this reading put it back with schist alone. Dark chocolate, in GRAPES, and cedar, from the French oak the Douro and Dao records name and the line itself names, make a fifth group, oak.
food.with.1.why: Deep fruit named nothing; blackberry does.
food.with.3.why: Fortified fruit named nothing; the Port's sweet black plum does.

questions.1.opts.3: Vinhao is Sousao, which the Codex's Douro trap names, and Sousao is a Port grape, so a distractor stood near the key of a question about the grape of Port. A Setubal red led by Castelao, no Port grape, takes its place.
open: Blueberry, in GRAPES and the lead, has no blue fruit group: one blue note alone cannot make one.
The Regionale trap calls Touriga Nacional Portugal's top red, a ranking the house keeps out of new prose.
